title: What We Lost When Big Tech Took Over the Classroom assroom
author: Jessica Winter
summary: Winter opens on a ransomware attack that shut down Springfield, Massachusetts schools for four days and left a district advising students and teachers to use books, notebooks and paper, a sentence she treats as diagnostic rather than quaint, since many American schools no longer have textbooks. Reviewing Natasha Singer's book Coding Kids, she argues the outage exposed something larger than weak cybersecurity: public schools have handed their curricula, pedagogy, and operating systems to a few trillion dollar companies, with Google's Chromebooks and Workspace functioning as the framework of K-12 education. She revisits the 2013 launch of Code.org, funded by Microsoft and Google and fronted by tech celebrities, and notes the organization had no lessons or product when its recruiting video went viral. The learn to code campaign, she contends, failed on its own terms, since generative AI has hollowed out the entry level programming jobs it promised, a reversal she illustrates with Obama's move from Code.org spokesman to advocate of a liberal arts education. Her deeper objection is philosophical, that the whole project rested on an unexamined premise that public schooling should be vocational and therefore aligned with corporate interests. She then tracks the current backlash, including Gemini's arrival on school Chromebooks, parental support for AI moratoria, and new restrictions in Los Angeles and New York, while cataloguing the loopholes that remain, teachers still using AI, assessment platforms exempt from screen limits, and a fresh round of AI pilots for high schoolers.
points: The Springfield ransomware shutdown works as the article's proof of dependency, since losing Microsoft 365 and PowerSchool removed schedules, assignments, readings, and quizzes at once.
Winter argues Google Workspace for Education is functionally the centralized student data project inBloom under another name, after inBloom itself collapsed under parental backlash in 2014.
She notes the learn to code push has been undone by the tech industry, with AI eliminating the entry level jobs that justified it, and cites Obama's reversal toward liberal arts.
Her strongest structural claim is that the coding campaign assumed without argument that public education should be vocational and aligned with corporate interests.
She details the inconsistency of the new AI restrictions, including teacher use, exempt assessment platforms like i-Ready, and five outside AI pilots reaching up to fifty thousand high schoolers.
quotes: In the midst of the crisis, the district circulated an F.A.Q. with a rather exotic recommendation: “Students and teachers may use books, notebooks and paper while technology teaching tools are restored.

But the emergency that the attack created also reflects how public schools in the U.S. have effectively surrendered much of their pedagogy, curricula, and operating systems to a handful of trillion-dollar technology companies.

Google and Apple and Microsoft have become the scaffolding on which many U.S. schools function,” Natasha Singer writes in her new book, “Coding Kids: Big Tech’s Battle to Remake Public Schools.” “The tech industry’s growing role in the classroom has become too big and too integral, it seems, to interrogate.

Kids who might have caught the programming bug during an Hour of Code in the twenty-tens are now entering a dismal market for recent computer-science graduates, as A.I. has made many entry-level tech jobs obsolete.

But that miscalculation was, itself, premised on the unexamined assumption that a K-12 public education should be essentially vocational and therefore—almost by definition—aligned with corporate interests.
In many respects, Google Workspace for Education—where students’ profile photos, passwords, grades, attendance records, e-mails, chat logs, and more can be stored—is inBloom by any other name.

Educators and policymakers are no longer making decisions about technology in the classroom, though they may feel like they are,” Emily Tavoulareas, an independent researcher who studies technology and public policy, stated in a recent address to the Fairfax County School Board, in Virginia.

A recent large study of Chinese students between the ages of twelve and eighteen found that, after six months of using A.I., they completed their homework assignments more accurately and much faster than before—but that their test scores were twenty per cent lower than those of peers who didn’t use A.I. to do their homework.
